title: Pauri 25, meaning: even hunger is a gift
hookLine: His generosity cannot be written; even pain and hunger are counted among His gifts (Japji 25)

lines: THE WORST YEAR OF YOUR LIFE.
cards: Ask someone about the worst year of their life, and then ask what came out of it. Sometimes there's a pause, and then something surprising. That's when I learned who my real friends were.
That's when I stopped drinking. That's when I found out I could survive. Nobody chooses a year like that.
Some still wouldn't give back what it taught them. Pauri 25 says something about hard things that's easy to misunderstand, so i'll go slowly.

teach.b: Today's word is daat: a gift, something given. Pauri 25 began: His generosity is so great it can't be written. Then it looks at everyone receiving, in paraphrase.
Many great warriors come begging at the Giver's door, and countless others, beyond counting. Some waste away in their own vices. Some take and take, then deny they ever received.
Some fools just keep on eating. Then the line: so many endure pain, hunger and constant blows.
In the original: eh bhi daat teree daataar. Even these are Your gifts, O Giver. What does that mean, and what doesn't it?
It doesn't mean hunger is fine, or that the hungry deserve it. Sikh life answers hunger by feeding people; that's what yesterday's langar is for. It doesn't tell anyone in pain to be quiet.
It says even the hard things come from the same hand, under the same Hukam, and can carry something in them.

Guru Nanak says it elsewhere, in the Asa di Vaar, in paraphrase: pain can be the medicine, and comfort the sickness. The stanza goes on: release from bondage comes by the divine will; no one else has a say.
The Giver knows, and the Giver gives. And the last lines: the one who is blessed to sing praise, Nanak says, is the king of kings.
So the stanza ends not on wealth, or even comfort, but on the gift of praise, which can come even in a hard year.

how: Pauri 25 is recited in the morning Japji Sahib; many Sikhs speak of accepting the bhaana, the divine will, in hard times, while also serving in the langar to feed the hungry.

o: a debt that must be paid back
a test sent as a punishment

games.q: what's inside Pauri 25 — tap the pairs.

s: Pauri 25 says the hungry deserve their hunger
it says even hard things come from the same hand; Sikh life answers hunger with langar.
Pauri 25 says even pain and hunger are among the Giver's gifts
Pauri 25 ends on the gift of praise
the one blessed to sing praise is the king of kings.

games.q: you're going through pain and hunger. what does Pauri 25 call it?
o: even this is Your gift, O Giver.
games.why: eh bhi daat teree daataar. not that hunger is fine, but that even hard things come from the same hand and can carry something.

practice: Bring to mind one difficulty, not the heaviest thing you carry, just something hard right now, and hold it gently without pretending it's good.
Ask quietly whether anything is inside it: something it's teaching you, someone it's brought closer, a strength it's showing.
If you find one small thing, rest with it; if you don't, that's all right too, and just breathe with the difficulty.

wordCard.voice: Daat. A gift. Pauri 25 counts even pain and hunger among the Giver's gifts, and ends on the gift of praise.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: daat, a gift; daataar is the Giver. Japji Pauri 25: eh bhi daat teree daataar.

carryVoice: Your line: even this is a gift. That doesn't make hard things easy; it says they can carry something. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 5 (Japji, Pauri 25, the rest of the stanza)
Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 469 (Asa di Vaar, Guru Nanak: dukh daaroo sukh rog bhaiaa)
